Motivation: Explore in-context retrieval on a corpus scale, particularly for large datasets and generalization beyond training sizes, an area under-researched in prior work.

Method: The authors introduce BlockSearch, a 0.6B language model retriever with architectural and training modifications, enabling significant length-generalization and new attention mechanisms to manage attention dilution.

Result: At the million-token scale, BlockSearch matches dense retrieval on standard benchmarks and outperforms concurrent models, achieving higher performance in diverse tasks requiring different similarity notions.

Conclusion: The study highlights in-context retrieval as a viable alternative to traditional retrieval methods, with a focus on addressing attention control challenges as corpus size increases.

Abstract: Language models (LMs) raise an intriguing alternative to vector-based retrieval: conditioning on an in-context corpus and directly generating a relevant answer. However, prior work has largely focused on proprietary systems or the smaller-scale reranking task, leaving corpus-scale in-context retrieval largely unexplored. In this work, we present the first systematic study of in-context retrieval on two scales practical retrievers demand: million-token corpora and length-generalization far beyond training-time sizes. We first introduce BlockSearch, a 0.6B LM retriever whose architectural and training modifications improve over prior LM baselines and length-generalize up to 10 times beyond its training regime. Nevertheless, retrieval still collapses under more extreme extrapolation. We trace this failure to an attention dilution effect: as the corpus grows, irrelevant documents dominate the softmax denominator, reducing the normalized mass on the gold document even when its pre-softmax score stays high. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce length-aware adjustments to the attention softmax and document-level sparse attention. With these modifications, at the million-token scale, our model matches dense retrieval on widely studied benchmarks (e.g, MS MARCO and NQ), while outperforming the concurrent model MSA despite being 7 times smaller. Furthermore, it significantly outperforms dense retrieval on tasks requiring entirely different notions of similarity, such as LIMIT, achieving a 3 times higher score. Together, our results position in-context retrieval a promising alternative to classical retrieval while emphasizing attention control under extreme context growth as a new challenge.

</details>


### [149] [DiPS: Dialogue Policy Selection for High-Stakes Persuasion Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01557)
*Tianyi Zhang,Mousumi Das,Abrar Anwar,Jesse Thomason,David Traum*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents DiPS, a Q-learning framework for adaptive persuasion in high-stakes contexts, specifically in fire evacuation scenarios, showing improved effectiveness over traditional LLMs and baseline methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enhance persuasion effectiveness in high-stakes situations, which require tailored strategies due to varying individual personalities and concerns.

Method: We propose Dialogue Policy Selection (DiPS), a Q-learning framework that selects persuasion strategies based on the evolving conversational context and the resident's recent utterances.

Result: DiPS demonstrated significantly higher evacuation success rates compared to zero-shot LLMs and generic RAG-augmented strategies in both simulated and real interactions.

Conclusion: The study concludes that dynamically adapting persuasion strategies through DiPS leads to better outcomes in critical evacuation scenarios.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with persuasion in high-stakes scenarios. People's individual personalities and concerns require tailored strategies rather than a one-size-fits-all approach. To address this challenge, we focus on a fire-rescue scenario in which an operator must persuade a resident to evacuate as a high-stakes persuasion domain and propose Dialogue Policy Selection (DiPS), a Q-learning framework to dynamically select persuasion strategies adapted to the evolving conversational context. Specifically, we train a critic, trained to maximize the chance of evacuation success, to select a persuasion policy at each turn based on the resident's recent utterances.We then evaluate DiPS against multiple baselines in both simulated and real human interactions. We find that DiPS achieves higher evacuation success than a zero-shot LLM and generic RAG-augmented approach.

</details>


### [150] [HaloGuard 1.0: An Open Weights Constitutional Classifier for Multilingual AI Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02079)
*Navaneeth Sangameswaran,Preetham S,Ashmiya Lenin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: HaloGuard 1.0 provides an open-weights implementation of the constitutional-classifier paradigm for enhanced input safety, showcasing superior performance on prompt-safety benchmarks while being significantly smaller than existing models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enhance input safety in model outputs using a structured constitutional framework, while overcoming size limitations of current leading models.

Method: Developed using a natural-language constitution comprising 46 policies and 2,940 subcategories, focusing on synthetic data generation with counterfactuals and a two-tier design to manage false positives.

Result: Achieved state-of-the-art performance with an F1 score of 90.9 for the 0.8B model and 92.1 for the 4B model, with low false-positive rates and effective multilingual capabilities.

Conclusion: HaloGuard 1.0 demonstrates that smaller models can achieve high safety performance, and ongoing adversarial protocols help ensure robust protection against various attacks.

Abstract: We present HaloGuard 1.0, an open-weights implementation of the constitutional-classifier paradigm for input safety. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on English and multilingual prompt-safety benchmarks at roughly one-tenth the model size of current leading open guard models. The safety constitution is the organising structure of the corpus: a natural-language constitution of 46 policies and 2,940 subcategories drives synthetic data generation, with exhaustive one-to-one paired counterfactuals that hold topic and vocabulary fixed while flipping intent, a two-tier harmless design that separately targets boundary and baseline false positives (FPs), and balanced multilingual materialisation across 46 languages that treats language as a surface form appearing on both sides of the boundary rather than as an adversarial signal. Across seven prompt-safety benchmarks, HaloGuard 1.0-0.8B attains the best average F1 (90.9) of any open guard we evaluate, outperforming baselines up to 27B parameters (over 30 times larger) while holding false-positive rate (FPR) to 4.3 and false-negative rate (FNR) to 9.5. The HaloGuard 1.0-4B variant reaches average F1 of 92.1 and FPR of 3.5, spending its extra capacity on precision rather than recall. A structured adjudication of the remaining failures indicates that most apparent missed-harm cases are benchmark mislabels rather than genuine model misses. An always-on adversarial red-teaming protocol continuously hardens the guard against both content-level and agentic attacks. We release the models as open weights.

</details>


### [151] [Beyond Skepticism: Evaluating LLMs Pedagogical Intent Reasoning with the Adaptive Pedagogical Vigilance Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01581)
*Minghao Chen,Ruihan Zhou,Jiayi Tang,Zihan Xu,Bowen Huang,Yuxin Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Adaptive Pedagogical Vigilance (APV) framework, enhancing Large Language Models' (LLMs) understanding of pedagogical intent in translation pedagogy through Bayesian reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explore LLMs' reasoning capability regarding pedagogical intent, focusing on optimizing learning in educational contexts.

Method: The Adaptive Pedagogical Vigilance (APV) framework uses a Bayesian Pedagogical Intent Inference Engine (PIIE) to model instructors' content selection and learners' reasoning about instructional configurations.

Result: APV significantly enhances model vigilance, achieving high correlation with human judgments (r=0.958) and outperforming baseline methods on naturalistic data.

Conclusion: This research creates a comprehensive framework for improving LLMs' comprehension of pedagogical motives, benefiting AI-assisted learning systems.

Abstract: The capacity of Large Language Models (LLMs) to reason about pedagogical intent within instructional communication remains underexplored, particularly in educational domains such as translation pedagogy. To address this, we propose the \textbf{Adaptive Pedagogical Vigilance (APV)} framework, a novel computational formalism that reframes communicative vigilance as an adaptive mechanism for optimizing learning through intent inference. APV formalizes the problem via a Bayesian Pedagogical Intent Inference Engine (PIIE), which models how instructors select content to maximize pedagogical utility and how vigilant learners should inversely reason about latent instructional configurations -- encompassing genre, stance, and incentives. We evaluate APV through a three-tier hierarchy: distinguishing instructional genre, reasoning about structured pedagogical setups, and generalizing to authentic educational discourse. Experiments on leading LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, Claude 3.5) show that APV substantially improves model vigilance. It achieves the strongest discrimination between pedagogical and exposure-based content, correlates highly with human judgments ($r=0.958$), and maintains robust performance on naturalistic data where baseline methods degrade. This work establishes a unified framework for assessing and enhancing LLMs' understanding of pedagogical motives, advancing the development of more reliable AI-assisted learning systems.

</details>


### [152] [ProWAFT: A ROMA-LPD Instance for Workload-Aware and Dynamic Fault Tolerance in FPGA-Based CNN Accelerators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01602)
*Xinxin Chen,Haoran Qiao,Yiming Guo,Kecheng Luo,Siyuan Feng,Jingwen Ma*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ProWAFT is a proactive fault-tolerance framework for SRAM-based FPGAs, optimizing CNN inference reliability by selectively applying TMR based on workload criticality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the reliability challenges of SRAM-based FPGAs in CNN inference while minimizing performance overheads associated with always-on redundancy and reactive recovery.

Method: ProWAFT utilizes partial reconfiguration to apply TMR to critical tasks based on a model that quantifies workload criticality, fault propagation, and reconfiguration costs.

Result: ProWAFT demonstrates lower composite costs compared to static TMR and reactive methods, achieving high success rates and throughput with minimal decision overhead.

Conclusion: The framework effectively balances latency, energy, and reliability, providing a robust solution for FPGA-based CNN acceleration in energy- and latency-constrained environments.

Abstract: SRAM-based FPGAs provide an attractive platform for energy- and latency-constrained CNN inference at the network edge, yet transient faults can lead to silent errors that compromise reliability. Always-on redundancy (e.g., full TMR) improves correctness but incurs substantial performance and energy overhead, while reactive recovery may introduce unacceptable latency on the critical path. We propose \textbf{ProWAFT}, a proactive workload-aware fault-tolerance framework for FPGA-based CNN accelerators that uses partial reconfiguration to selectively apply TMR across reconfigurable partitions. ProWAFT quantifies workload criticality, models fault propagation and reconfiguration overhead, and selects configurations that minimize a composite objective over latency, energy, and reliability risk. Implemented on a Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ ZCU104 platform with six reconfigurable regions and evaluated on a 500-task trace derived from ResNet-18, MobileNetV2, and EfficientNet-Lite under time-varying SEU injection, ProWAFT achieves lower composite cost than static TMR and reactive reconfiguration while maintaining high task success rate and near-baseline throughput with low online decision overhead.

</details>


### [153] [When Does Generating More Help? Disentangling Fixed-Source Synthesis from Source Expansion in Synthetic Data Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01727)
*Xu Guo,Jian Tong,Zhihui Lu,Qipeng Guo*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS) in synthetic data generation by isolating it from Source Expansion (SE). The study derives a scaling law specific to FSS, demonstrating its performance at varying budgets, and finds that, at large budgets, SE outperforms FSS.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the underexplored area of Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS) in synthetic data generation by isolating its effects from Source Expansion (SE).

Method: The authors fix the seed-question pool and teacher model while varying the response budget using Rejection Sampling (RS) and adapt the rectified scaling law specifically for FSS.

Result: The derived scaling law predicts performance effectively at high budgets and shows that FSS is comparable to SE at small budgets; at large budgets, SE outperforms FSS when additional seed questions are integrated.

Conclusion: FSS serves as a bounded scaling axis for comparing synthesis protocols, with recommendations to enable further research through code and data release.

Abstract: Synthetic data can be scaled along two routes: Source Expansion (SE), which enlarges the source by adding seed materials or generators, and Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS), which holds the source fixed and scales the generation budget. Existing scaling studies typically expand the source as the data grows, conflating SE with FSS and leaving FSS underexplored. We isolate FSS by holding the seed-question pool and teacher model fixed, varying only the per-question response budget under Rejection Sampling (RS). We adapt the rectified scaling law to FSS, deriving it from how repeated sampling covers a fixed source. Empirically, the derived form, fit on low budgets, predicts performance at the held-out highest budget for every evaluated teacher--student pair. At matched total-sample budgets, SE and FSS are comparable at small budgets; at large budgets, adding seed questions outperforms spending the same budget on more responses. Within FSS, however, neither synthesizing additional questions from the existing seeds nor varying the synthesis protocol outperforms plain RS at matched budgets. FSS is thus a bounded scaling axis and a controlled setting for comparing synthesis protocols. We will release our code and data to facilitate further research.

</details>


### [154] [Rethinking Speech-LLM Integration for ASR: Effective Joint Speech-Text Training by Interleaving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01733)
*Ruchao Fan,Yiming Wang,Rui Zhao,Liliang Ren,Keqi Deng,Xiaoyang Chen,Ali Zare,Bo Ren,Yuxuan Hu,Junkun Chen,Yan Huang,Yelong Shen,Jinyu Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes a new pretraining strategy, Joint Speech-Text Interleaved Pretraining (JSTIP), for improving automatic speech recognition (ASR) by interleaving speech and text sequences, leading to better entity recognition performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To clarify the benefits of Large Language Models (LLMs) for ASR and address the under-utilization of textual knowledge in joint training, especially as ASR training data increases.

Method: JSTIP introduces a strategy that constructs interleaved word-level and segment-level speech-text sequences from aligned pairs, specifically designed for architectures that take continuous speech inputs.

Result: Experiments indicate that JSTIP consistently improves entity accuracy compared to ASR-only and traditional joint speech-text training methods, achieving competitive performance with existing ASR and Speech-LLM systems for medical entity recognition.

Conclusion: The interleaving approach helps bridge the gap between speech and text modalities, preserving LLM generative properties and enhancing performance in ASR tasks.

Abstract: Speech-LLM integration has shown promising results by leveraging extensive textual pretraining, yet its specific benefits for automatic speech recognition (ASR) remain unclear. We observe that as supervised ASR training data increases, the contribution of LLM priors becomes less evident, and simple speech-text joint training under-utilizes textual knowledge. We therefore propose Joint Speech-Text Interleaved Pretraining (JSTIP), an ASR-oriented pretraining strategy that constructs word-level and segment-level interleaved speech-text sequences within aligned pairs for speech-LLM architectures that accept continuous inputs. Experiments on 38k hours of ASR data show consistent entity accuracy improvement compared to ASR-only and joint speech-text training baselines. JSTIP achieves on-par entity recognition performance using domain transcription text compared to synthetic speech-text pairs, simplifying domain adaptation. Benefiting from textual pretraining and domain text data, JSTIP is competitive with open-source ASR and Speech-LLM systems in medical entity recognition. The zero-shot speech question answering behaviors further suggest that interleaving reduces the speech-text modality gap and preserves the LLM generative prior, which is likely the reason for the entity improvements on the ASR task.

</details>


### [155] [PARTREP: Learning What to Repeat for Decoder-only LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01792)
*Andikawati P Widjaja,Yongjun Kim,Hyounghun Kim,Jaeho Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PartRep enhances decoder-only LLM performance by selectively appending the most informative tokens of prompts, reducing computational costs compared to full prompt repetition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The study addresses the issue of asymmetric information flow in decoder-only LLMs caused by causal attention, leading to an imbalance in contextual grounding among tokens.

Method: PartRep utilizes token-wise negative log-likelihood (NLL) for selecting the most informative prompt tokens to append, avoiding the need for a full forward pass by employing a trained gate that predicts high-NLL tokens from early-layer hidden states during mid-prefill.

Result: PartRep demonstrates competitive performance on multiple benchmarks and model families, achieving significant reductions in KV cache usage and prefill FLOPs while retaining most performance gains from full prompt repetition.

Conclusion: The proposed method effectively balances improved reasoning performance with practical computational efficiency in long-context scenarios.

Abstract: While decoder-only LLMs excel at a vast array of natural language tasks, it suffers from an asymmetric information flow induced by causal attention: later tokens are richer in contextual grounding than earlier ones. A simple and effective remedy is prompt repetition -- just appending a second copy of prompt before generation can redistribute grounding across positions and improve reasoning performance. However, full repetition of the original prompt doubles the KV cache footprint and quadruples attention cost during prefill, making it impractical for long-context settings. We propose PartRep, a selective augmentation method that appends only the most informative tokens -- rather than the entire prompt. We use token-wise negative log-likelihood (NLL) as a selection signal, motivated by the hypothesis that less predictable tokens are less recoverable from surrounding context and therefore benefit more from late-position repetition. To avoid the heavy cost of a full forward pass for scoring, we train a lightweight gate that predicts high-NLL tokens from early-layer hidden states, enabling token selection during mid-prefill via early exit. Across eight benchmarks (including MMLU, GSM8K, and RULER) and three model families (Qwen2.5, Llama3.2, Gemma4), PartRep retains most of the gains of full repetition while using only 59.4\% of its KV cache and 79.0\% of its prefill FLOPs.

</details>


### [156] [On the Limits of Steering Vectors for Preference-Aligned Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01802)
*Melanie Subbiah,Zara Hall,Kathleen McKeown*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper examines the effectiveness and limitations of steering vectors for controlled text generation, focusing on their applicability across various traits and tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need to improve controlled text generation mechanisms while understanding the generalizability of steering vectors in different contexts.

Method: The study utilizes the PLUME benchmark to evaluate steering vectors extracted for different preferences on summarization and email-writing tasks using two open-source models.

Result: Steering effectiveness is inconsistent across various traits, and transferring vectors from positive/negative examples can degrade performance; combining multiple vectors leads to drops in trait expression.

Conclusion: Steering vectors show significant limitations as a versatile tool for preference alignment in text generation.

Abstract: Steering vectors have emerged as a promising approach to controlled text generation, offering interpretable, training-free mechanisms for shaping model outputs. However, their practical generality remains poorly understood. We study the limits of steering vector generalization along three dimensions: trait expressibility, task transfer, and multi-trait composition. Using the PLUME writing personalization benchmark, we extract steering vectors for a range of preferences and evaluate them on summarization and email-writing tasks across two open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct). We find that steering effectiveness varies substantially across traits. We further show that steering effectiveness can degrade when vectors extracted from positive and negative style examples are transferred to downstream writing personalization tasks. Finally, we compare common methods for composing multiple steering vectors and find that all methods suffer significant drops in trait expression as more vectors are added, with a tradeoff between coherence and expressibility that requires per-setting hyperparameter tuning. Taken together, our results suggest that steering vectors face meaningful limits as a general-purpose tool for preference alignment.

</details>


### [157] [PairCoder++: Pair Programming as a Universal Paradigm for Verified Code-Driven Multimodal and Structured-Artifact Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01883)
*Junhao Chen,Xiang Li,Mingjin Chen,Boran Zhang,Henghaofan Zhang,Yibin Xu,Yuehan Cui,Fangsheng Weng,Fei Ma,Qi Tian,Ruqi Huang,Hao Zhao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PairCoder enhances large language model output quality through a dual-agent system that integrates program writing and reviewing, leading to significant improvements in verifiable artifacts across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for more reliable and verifiable outputs from large language models when generating structured artifacts is paramount due to the limitations of single pass inference.

Method: PairCoder employs two agents in a pair programming setup: a Driver agent writes the code and a Navigator agent reviews it against various verification evidence. They alternate roles to resolve persistent errors.

Result: PairCoder shows consistent improvements across 17 public benchmarks and seven models from different vendors, significantly enhancing the quality of verifiable artifacts compared to single model approaches, with notable performance gains in specific contexts.

Conclusion: Pair programming, as implemented in PairCoder, effectively aids in generating verified code-driven artifacts, especially when the verification toolchain provides useful feedback.

Abstract: Code is the medium through which large language models generate structured artifacts: charts, scientific figures, vector graphics, CAD models, 3D scenes, and hardware designs are all produced by writing programs. In this regime single pass inference is brittle, because the compiler, renderer, or simulator that decides whether the artifact exists is invisible to the model. We present PairCoder, which grounds review in the toolchain and realizes it as two agent pair programming: a Driver agent writes the program, a Navigator agent reviews it against verification evidence (diagnostics, execution results, and renderings of the current artifact beside the target), and the two switch roles when errors persist. Across 17 public benchmarks and seven models from three vendors, PairCoder improves essentially every benchmark whose artifact is verifiable, on full official metric suites rather than execution alone (for example, Blender scene executability 0.20 to 0.78; TikZ compile rate up 10 to 30 points on every model), at 2.9 to 9.2 times single model cost (about 7 times overall). The improvements concentrate where the toolchain provides an informative oracle and the baseline leaves headroom, and the method ties or mildly regresses where the oracle is weak; we frame pair programming as a reliable recipe for verified code driven generation.

</details>


### [158] [The Grammar Does the Work: Functional vs. Lexical Dependency Length Minimization Across Universal Dependencies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01899)
*Kim Gerdes*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The study analyzes dependency length minimization (DLM) across 122 languages, revealing two levels of optimization: grammar-driven for functional dependencies and processing-driven for lexical dependencies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the obscured variation in dependency distances across syntactic relation types, which previous studies overlooked by reporting a single mean dependency distance per language.

Method: Analyzed 122 languages from Universal Dependencies and Singapore Universal Dependencies databases to evaluate how DLM operates differently on functional vs. lexical dependencies.

Result: Functional dependencies are universally short and consistent across diverse languages (mean 1.71), whereas lexical dependencies are longer, more variable, and influenced by word-order typology (mean 2.87).

Conclusion: The grammar facilitates minimization through local functional attachments, while processing pressures dictate the arrangement of lexical heads.

Abstract: Dependency length minimization (DLM) is a well-documented processing universal, but previous studies report a single mean dependency distance (MDD) per language, obscuring variation across syntactic relation types. We analyze 122 languages in UD and SUD (version 2.17), showing that DLM operates on two distinct levels. Grammar-driven optimization targets functional dependencies (det, case, aux), which are universally short (mean 1.71, $σ$ = 0.33) and invariant across typologically diverse languages. Processing-driven optimization operates on lexical dependencies (nsubj, obj, obl), which are longer (mean 2.87), highly variable ($σ$ = 0.63), and constrained by word-order typology. This asymmetry holds in SUD despite reversed head direction (r = 0.92). We conclude that ''the grammar does the work'' of minimization by scaffolding sentences with local functional attachments, leaving processing pressures to determine the ordering of lexical heads.

</details>


### [159] [TUDUM: A Turkish-Thinking Reasoning Pipeline for Qwen3.5-27B](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01927)
*Baran Bingol,Bahaeddin Turkoglu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces TUDUM, a Turkish adaptation of the Qwen-family 27B model that focuses on explicit Turkish reasoning, utilizing supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to address mixed performance outcomes in reasoning tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop a thinking model that processes and reasons in Turkish, addressing limitations in existing models that primarily operate in English and only localize final outputs.

Method: The pipeline begins with the unsloth/Qwen3.5-27B base model, employs supervised fine-tuning on 15,991 Turkish reasoning examples with LoRA adapters, and utilizes GRPO-family reinforcement learning within a Turkish mathematics environment.

Result: Supervised fine-tuning improved the model's Turkish reasoning consistency but reduced benchmark accuracy; reinforcement learning enhanced some mathematical performance but did not outperform the base model on all benchmarks.

Conclusion: TUDUM serves as an honest technical advancement in Turkish reasoning, with publicly available models, rather than claiming state-of-the-art proficiency.

Abstract: This paper presents TUDUM (Türkçe Düşünen Üretken Model), a project pipeline for adapting a Qwen-family 27B thinking model toward Turkish reasoning. The central problem is not only to answer Turkish prompts in Turkish, but to make the explicit reasoning trace itself Turkish. A thinking model may translate a Turkish prompt into an English-centered internal or visible scratchpad, solve the problem mostly in English, and only localize the final answer. TUDUM instead treats the generated <think>...</think> block as a trainable behavior. The pipeline starts from the project base checkpoint unsloth/Qwen3.5-27B, applies supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on 15,991 Turkish reasoning examples using LoRA adapters, and then applies GRPO-family reinforcement learning on a proxy-filtered Turkish mathematics environment. The results are mixed. SFT made the model shorter and more consistently Turkish in its reasoning behavior, with large reductions in average response length and thinking exhaustion, but reduced benchmark accuracy. RL recovered some mathematical performance, especially AIME24 at the best early checkpoint, yet did not uniformly improve all benchmarks and did not exceed the base model on the reported Macro-6 average. The contribution is therefore best framed as a technically honest Turkish-thinking reasoning pipeline and evaluation, not as a claim of state-of-the-art Turkish reasoning. The released step-50 model is publicly available.

</details>


### [160] [NAVER LABS Europe Submission to the Instruction-following 2026 Short Track](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01960)
*Marcely Zanon Boito,Hemant Yadav,Jean-Luc Meunier,Ioan Calapodescu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: NAVER LABS Europe achieves top ranking in IWSLT 2026 by enhancing a speech processing system for ASR, ST, and SQA tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve the performance and efficiency of speech processing tasks in a competitive environment.

Method: Developed a multi-stage training pipeline incorporating SpeechMapper for speech-to-LLM embedding and created a synthetic SQA dataset, fakACL, from generated scientific presentations.

Result: The updated model surpasses last year's best system in performance, achieving a tied first-place ranking overall in the short track.

Conclusion: The integration of advanced training methods and domain-specific data has resulted in significant performance improvements despite a more compact system.

Abstract: In this paper, we describe NAVER LABS Europe's submission to the instruction-following speech processing short track at IWSLT 2026. We participate again in the constrained setting, developing systems capable of jointly performing ASR, ST, and SQA from English speech into Chinese, Italian, and German. Building on our previous submission, ranked first in last year's short track, we update our multi-stage training pipeline by replacing the speech projector with SpeechMapper, a method for learning a speech-to-LLM embedding projector using only ASR data. In addition, we introduce a synthetic SQA dataset, fakACL, composed of artificially generated scientific presentations. This dataset is built by prompting the LLM backbone, segmenting the generated talks, and synthesizing speech with SeamlessM4T-large-v2. The combination of an improved speech projection mechanism and domain-specific synthetic data allows our model to outperform last year's best short-track system, while being considerably more compact and relying on a weaker LLM backbone. This year's results place our system tied for first place in the overall short track ranking.

</details>


### [161] [Beyond Supervised Clarification: Input Rewriting with LLMs for Dialogue Discourse Parsing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01964)
*Yiming Liu,Ziyue Zhang,Zhichao Xu,Xin Yu,Yingheng Tang,Tianyu Jiang,Jie Cao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This study evaluates the effectiveness of rewriting inputs to enhance parsing accuracy in dialogue discourse parsing without supervision, revealing significant limitations and proposing rewritability prediction as a crucial improvement area.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To assess the practical effectiveness of rewriting inputs for improving the accuracy of downstream DDP models under realistic deployment conditions where clarification supervision is unavailable.

Method: The research analyzed the performance of last-utterance clarification and parser-agnostic rewriting across multiple SDRT datasets and parsers. It also tested a parser-aware clarifier trained with GRPO.

Result: The analysis showed that parser-agnostic rewriting led to more inaccuracies than repairs, with many errors remaining unfixable through input rewriting. The parser-aware clarifier improved regressions by up to 37%, yet failed to provide consistently effective clarifications.

Conclusion: Clarification should be viewed as a selective intervention problem, emphasizing the importance of predicting rewritability to optimize frozen discourse parsers and enhance agentic NLP pipelines.

Abstract: Rewriting inputs to improve frozen downstream models has become a common strategy in modern NLP pipelines. Prior work on incremental dialogue discourse parsing (DDP) shows that supervised clarification models can rewrite fragmentary or underspecified utterances, such as resolving ellipsis or references, to improve parsing accuracy. In this work, we revisit this idea under realistic deployment conditions, where no clarification supervision is available and the clarifier must rely on zero-shot prompting or feedback from a frozen parser. Across three Segmented Discourse Representation Theory (SDRT) datasets and multiple parsers, we find that last-utterance clarification is far less reliable than suggested by supervised settings. Parser-agnostic rewriting often introduces more regressions than repairs, as edits that enable fixes also disrupt discourse cues relied upon by the parser. A best-of-8 rewriting analysis further reveals a practical ceiling: a large fraction of errors are not repairable through input rewriting alone. A parser-aware clarifier trained with GRPO reduces regressions by up to 37% by learning conservative abstention, yet still fails to produce selectivity-aware clarifications that consistently improve parsing. Together, these findings recast clarification as a selective intervention problem. We identify rewritability prediction, deciding whether an utterance is repairable before intervention, as the key missing capability for input-side optimization of frozen discourse parsers, and a critical direction for improving agentic pipelines more broadly.

</details>


### [162] [Towards a Phonology-Informed Evaluation of Multilingual TTS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01965)
*Sneha Ray Barman,Neeraj Kumar Sharma,Shakuntala Mahanta*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The study proposes a framework to audit Neural TTS systems for phonological accuracy, revealing discrepancies in vowel harmony in Assamese TTS outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research highlights the inadequacy of existing metrics, like MOS, in assessing phonological sound contrasts in TTS systems, emphasizing the need for a more effective auditing method.

Method: The study introduces a classifier-based framework that compares synthesized TTS output with human speech, focusing on specific phonological patterns such as Assamese ATR vowel harmony.

Result: The classifier successfully identifies phonological discrepancies in TTS outputs, with notable findings such as the misrepresentation of ATR vowels in synthesized speech and a superior classification accuracy of predicted ATR labels over transcription labels.

Conclusion: The proposed framework not only provides insights into specific phonological issues in TTS systems but also offers potential for application to a wider range of phonological contrasts.

Abstract: Neural TTS systems can sound natural across languages, but naturalness does not guarantee the preservation of sound contrasts that distinguish words from their grammatical forms. Standard metrics like MOS do not test for this. We propose a classifier-based framework that audits TTS output against language-specific phonological patterns using human speech as a benchmark. Testing Assamese advanced tongue root (ATR) vowel harmony with Meta's MMS TTS, we show that a classifier trained on human speech transfers to synthesized speech with minimal loss. The faithfulness audit reveals that [+ATR] mid vowels are realized as [-ATR] in 1/3 tokens despite an underlying [+ATR] specification, a bias absent in human speech. At the word level, predicted ATR labels classify harmony more accurately than transcription labels, indicating a gap between intended and produced phonology. The framework offers task-specific diagnostics and generalizes to other phonological contrasts with measurable acoustic cues.

</details>


### [163] [Object Aligner: A Configurable JSON Schema Similarity Score for Graphs, Applied to LLM Prompt Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01972)
*Jan Drchal*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Object Aligner (OA) is a library for scoring JSON outputs based on schema conformity using tree alignment and referential alignment to handle complex structured data efficiently.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to enhance the accuracy of measuring how closely JSON outputs from LLMs conform to a fixed schema, overcoming limitations of existing metrics like exact match and text similarity.

Method: The method involves using a library that recursively aligns JSON trees, applying algorithms such as the Hungarian algorithm and Weisfeiler-Leman color refinement for scoring, while allowing schema adaptations through JSON Schema extensions.

Result: The Object Aligner's referential alignment approach infers identifier mappings, providing scores invariant to relabeling, and can emit ranked repair suggestions without additional cost.

Conclusion: Integrated with the GEPA prompt optimizer, the Object Aligner demonstrates effectiveness and neutrality across various datasets.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often asked to produce JSON conforming to a fixed schema, powering information extraction, tool calling, agentic planning, and knowledge-graph construction. Measuring how closely an output matches a gold reference is essential yet surprisingly hard: exact match is brittle, text similarity ignores structure, and an LLM judge is expensive, opaque, and non-deterministic. We address this with Object Aligner (OA), an open-source Python library that scores two JSON objects deterministically by recursively aligning their trees (the Hungarian algorithm for unordered collections, sequence alignment for ordered ones) and awarding partial credit at the granularity the schema declares. The Object Aligner is configured entirely through a set of JSON Schema extensions, so adapting it to a new task involves annotating a schema rather than writing code. Complex structured data, however, are rarely flat trees: records may form graphs or hypergraphs keyed by arbitrary identifiers, breaking the assumptions of prior similarity metrics. Our central contribution, referential alignment, closes this gap by inferring a bijection between gold and candidate identifiers and scoring every reference through it, so the score is invariant to relabeling. Since recovering this bijection exactly is graph isomorphism, the Object Aligner approximates it with Weisfeiler-Leman color refinement. An order-sensitive sequence regime targets ranking and planning. Since the same alignment localizes every mismatch, the Object Aligner emits ranked repair suggestions at no extra cost. Used as a reward inside the GEPA prompt optimizer, Object Aligner helps or stays neutral across all datasets.

</details>


### [164] [Using embeddings to predict spoken word duration and pitch in Mandarin monosyllabic words](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02002)
*Xiaoyun Jin,Mirjam Ernestus,R. Harald Baayen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The study demonstrates that contextualized embeddings can predict spoken duration of Mandarin monosyllabic words effectively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explore the predictive capability of contextualized embeddings regarding spoken word duration in Mandarin.

Method: Analysis of 7470 Mandarin monosyllabic CV words, employing type-wise and token-wise permutations to validate the predictions from contextualized embeddings.

Result: CEs predict word duration significantly above chance, applicable at both type and token levels, with precise predictions enabling conversion of normalized f0 contours to accurate ms-scaled contours.

Conclusion: The predicted contours closely resemble empirical data and surpass a permutation baseline in performance.

Abstract: Time-normalized f0 contours of Mandarin words in conversational speech have been shown to be predictable in part from their contextualized embeddings (CEs). The present study investigates whether CEs also predict spoken word duration for 7470 tokens of Mandarin monosyllabic CV words extracted from a Mandarin corpus of spontaneous speech. We show that CEs indeed are predictive for duration, above chance level, not only at the type level, but also at the level of individual tokens, as indicated by the results obtained with the type-wise and token-wise permutation baselines. We also show that the predicted durations are sufficiently precise to back-transform predicted f0 contours in [0,1] normalized time to contours on the ms time scale. The resulting predicted contours approximate empirical contours and also outperform a permutation baseline.

</details>


### [165] [EduArt: An educational-level benchmark for evaluating art history knowledge in large language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02007)
*Gianmarco Spinaci,Lukas Klic,Giovanni Colavizza*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: EduArt benchmark assesses multimodal LLMs on art-historical knowledge and visual reasoning with 871 human-authored questions in various formats. It reveals that recognition formats can overestimate model capabilities, indicating a need for diverse evaluations in art history contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate how models perform specifically in art-historical knowledge and visual reasoning, as existing benchmarks fail to capture item-level properties and rely on synthetic evaluations.

Method: Utilized 871 questions from Italian secondary-school exercises and US AP Art History exams, covering multiple formats and languages, to assess twelve models from six provider families under varying conditions.

Result: The benchmark demonstrated strong psychometric properties, but models performed significantly worse on open completion and error identification compared to multiple-choice, with motivation conditions generally decreasing accuracy.

Conclusion: Art-historical knowledge and application are distinct skills, thus relying on single-format benchmarks can overestimate model capabilities, emphasizing the need for a diverse evaluation framework in art-historical research.

Abstract: Large language models now score near ceiling on general benchmarks, but these aggregate measures reveal little about how models behave within single disciplines. Existing art-focused evaluations rely on synthetic questions and rarely report item-level properties. This paper introduces EduArt, an educational-level benchmark for art-historical knowledge and visual reasoning in multimodal LLMs. EduArt comprises 871 human-authored questions from Italian secondary-school exercises and US Advanced Placement Art History exams, spanning two languages and seven formats from multiple choice to in-text word placement and error identification. Twelve models from six provider families were evaluated under a default answer-only condition and a motivation condition requiring written justification, and characterized using Classical Test Theory and a logistic regression isolating the effects of format, language, image presence, and model. The benchmark showed strong psychometric properties (mean discrimination 0.514, 82.3 percent good discriminators), while multiple-choice accuracy saturated near ceiling for six models, showing recognition formats alone cannot distinguish frontier models. Format was a strong independent predictor of accuracy: models exceeding 94 percent on multiple choice fell to 23.9 percent on open completion (Claude Opus 4.6) and 6.2 percent on error identification (Claude Sonnet 4.6). The motivation condition changed accuracy in a predominantly negative, family-dependent direction. These dissociations indicate that art-historical knowledge and the ability to deploy it are distinct capabilities, and that single-format benchmarks overestimate what models can reliably do. Mapping this capability profile is a precondition for responsible use of multimodal LLMs in art-historical scholarship, where tasks demand producing and manipulating content rather than selecting from fixed options.

</details>


### [166] [OpenSafeIntent: Evaluating Intent-Calibrated Safe Completion Across Dual-Use Prompt Sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02047)
*Rheeya Uppaal,Seungwoo Lyu,Selina Sung,Junjie Hu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces OpenSafeIntent, a benchmark for evaluating model safety by testing intent variations across consistent tasks, revealing models' failures in maintaining safety under different intents and suggesting a need for intent-calibrated safety evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation behind this paper is to enhance the assessment of model safety by going beyond isolated prompts and focusing on intent variations in controlled tasks.

Method: The authors developed OpenSafeIntent, a benchmark consisting of controlled prompt-sets with benign, dual-use, and malicious variants of the same task to evaluate model responses across different intents.

Result: The findings reveal that models often fail to ensure safety when intent varies, display fragility in dual-use scenarios under paraphrased prompts, and generally provide unreliable safe responses to high-level queries on sensitive topics.

Conclusion: The research concludes that safety evaluations should account for intent variations and be framed as intent-calibrated behavior rather than a simplistic safety-helpfulness tradeoff.

Abstract: Safe completion requires models to provide useful assistance without enabling harm, but this behavior is difficult to evaluate with isolated prompts. We introduce OpenSafeIntent, a benchmark of controlled prompt-sets that vary intent while holding the underlying task fixed. Each datapoint contains benign, dual-use, and malicious variants of the same task. This design lets us evaluate whether models calibrate assistance across intent shifts, rather than merely appearing safe on average. Across a broad model suite, we find that prompt-level safety hides important failures: models often fail to remain safe across matched intent variants, dual-use behavior is brittle under paraphrase, high-level answers on risky topics are not reliably safe, and responses that reframe ambiguous requests into safer tasks are substantially less likely to cross the safety boundary. Our results suggest that safe completion should be evaluated as intent-calibrated behavior over controlled task variants, not as a single safety-helpfulness tradeoff over independent prompts.

</details>


### [167] [SPLIT: Cross-Lingual Empathy and Cultural Grounding in English and Ukrainian LLM Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02049)
*Anna Chorna*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper presents SPLIT, a benchmark assessing large language models (LLMs) in generating emotionally grounded responses during crises in multiple languages, particularly English and Ukrainian.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the underexplored cross-lingual abilities of LLMs in emotional-support contexts, particularly in low-to-mid-resource languages, and to examine their performance in crisis-related empathy and cultural grounding.

Method: The authors introduced the SPLIT benchmark comprising 500 prompts across five emotional categories and evaluated three LLMs based on Empathetic Accuracy, Linguistic Naturalness, and Contextual & Cultural Grounding.

Result: The evaluation found that while Gemini-2.5-Flash and LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct performance deteriorated in Ukrainian, DeepSeek-V3 showed stability. Human and AI evaluators expressed weak agreement on empathy and naturalness but diverged significantly on cultural grounding.

Conclusion: The results emphasize that producing text in Ukrainian does not equate to delivering effective Ukrainian emotional support, advocating for culturally tailored benchmarks and stronger human-centered evaluation in future LLM developments.

Abstract: Large Language Models are increasingly deployed in emotional-support contexts and crisis-related situations. Nevertheless, their cross-lingual abilities in these circumstances remain underexplored. Existing benchmarks emphasize multilingual performance but rarely examine crisis-related empathy and cultural grounding in low-to-mid-resource languages. We introduce SPLIT, a 500-prompt benchmark designed to evaluate LLM consistency in generating emotionally grounded responses across five categories: Stress, Panic, Loneliness, Internal Displacement, and Tension. We evaluate three technically diverse LLMs across three dimensions: Empathetic Accuracy, Linguistic Naturalness, and Contextual & Cultural Grounding. The framework aims to assess and compare the quality of LLM responses in both English and Ukrainian languages, as well as to explore the reliability of the LLM-as-a-jury paradigm. Our findings reveal that Gemini-2.5-Flash and LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct degrade when transitioning to Ukrainian, while DeepSeek-V3 remains comparatively stable within our benchmark. We additionally find that human and AI evaluators agree weakly on empathy and naturalness but diverge on cultural grounding. We further argue that producing Ukrainian text is not equivalent to producing Ukrainian emotional support. Our findings may assist in the future development of more culturally tailored benchmark designs, as well as encourage a stronger emphasis on human-centered evaluation.

</details>


### [168] [Unlocking Speech-Text Compositional Powers: Instruction-Following Speech Language Models without Instruction Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02214)
*Congrui Du,Yang Zhang,Kaizhi Qian,Shiyu Chang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces SpeechCombine, a novel method for training speech language models (SLMs) without instruction tuning, using a single round of speech pre-training on 30k hours of data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the challenges of instruction tuning for speech language models, which differ significantly from text-based models due to the complexity of speech modalities and longer sequence lengths.

Method: The method involves starting with a text large language model (LLM), performing continuous pre-training on speech data, and then combining the weights from the text LLM with the weight differences between the instruction-tuned and base versions of the text LLM.

Result: The combination strategy effectively retains the knowledge of the original text LLM while transferring its capabilities to the speech domain without the need for extensive speech data.

Conclusion: The findings indicate a promising new direction for SLM training that reduces reliance on large speech instruction tuning datasets.

Abstract: Instruction tuning for speech language models (SLMs) is substantially more challenging than for text-based large language models (LLMs), as it requires learning a new modality and a wide range of speech-specific instructions in addition to those supported by text LLMs. Existing SLM training approaches largely replicate the text LLM training paradigm by synthesizing large-scale speech pre-training and instruction-tuning datasets. However, this strategy is difficult to scale, since speech sequences are significantly longer than text sequences. In this paper, we propose SpeechCombine, an instruction-following speech language model trained without any instruction tuning, using only a single round of speech pre-training on 30k hours of data. Starting from a text LLM base model, we perform continuous pre-training on speech utterances to obtain a speech-adapted model, and then directly combine its weights with the weight difference between the instruction-tuned and base versions of the text LLM. Our results show that this simple combination strategy not only preserves the knowledge and capabilities of the original text LLM, but also effectively transfers them to the speech domain. These findings suggest a new direction for SLM training that avoids reliance on massive speech data.

</details>


### [169] [Challenges and Recommendations for LLMs-as-a-Judge in Multilingual Settings and Low-Resource Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02235)
*A. Seza Doğruöz,Xixian Liao,Verena Blaschke,Jakob Prange,Senyu Li,David Ifeoluwa Adelani*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes the application of LLM-as-a-Judge in evaluating multilingual and low-resource languages, finding limited focus and consistent issues in current methodologies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate the effectiveness and challenges of using LLMs as evaluators in multilingual contexts, particularly for low-resource languages, where human validation is often lacking.

Method: An analysis of 650 ACL Anthology papers mentioning LLM-as-a-Judge, focusing on the 33 addressing multilingual and low-resource challenges.

Result: The study reveals inconsistent evaluation outcomes, overreliance on LLM judgments, and a prevalent use of a single judge model in these studies.

Conclusion: Recommendations are provided for improving the implementation of LLM-as-a-Judge to better support evaluations in multilingual and low-resource language settings.

Abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge has become the dominant evaluation paradigm for many natural language generation tasks, due to shortcomings of conventional metrics and high correlations with human judgment, albeit mostly in English. There are now attempts to extend LLM-as-a-Judge to multilingual settings including low-resource languages. However, LLMs have limited proficiency in low-resource languages, and there is often no adequate human validation in these settings. To highlight the scope of the problem and current practices, we explore the use of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators in ACL Anthology papers focusing on multilingual settings and low-resource languages across a diverse set of tasks. Out of 650 papers mentioning LLM-as-a-judge, only 33 of them focus on low-resource or multilingual settings. Our in-depth analysis of these papers indicates inconsistent evaluation outcomes, a tendency to overtrust LLM judgments in multilingual settings, and the widespread reliance on a single judge model per study. To help the NLP community further, we conclude with recommendations about how to use LLM-as-a-Judge in multilingual and low-resource settings.

</details>


### [170] [BamiBERT: A New BERT-based Language Model for Vietnamese](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02259)
*Dat Quoc Nguyen,Thinh Pham,Chi Tran,Linh The Nguyen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: BamiBERT is a new Vietnamese language model outperforming PhoBERT, achieving state-of-the-art results across various benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address limitations in the current Vietnamese language model, PhoBERT.

Method: BamiBERT is trained on a 129GB corpus of Vietnamese text for 20 epochs, with an extended context length of 2048 tokens and no external word segmentation.

Result: BamiBERT achieved the best score on 11 of 15 metrics across 8 Vietnamese benchmarks, with second-best on 3 others.

Conclusion: BamiBERT sets a new state of the art for 'base'-sized Vietnamese encoders and demonstrates strong cross-domain generalization.

Abstract: In this paper, we introduce BamiBERT, a new BERT-based pre-trained language model for Vietnamese that addresses key limitations of PhoBERT -- the current de facto Vietnamese text encoder. Trained from scratch on a 129GB corpus of general-domain Vietnamese text for 20 epochs, BamiBERT supports an extended context length of up to 2048 tokens and operates directly on raw input, eliminating the need for external word segmentation. Across 8 Vietnamese benchmarks, it achieves the best score on 11 of 15 metrics and the second-best on 3 others, setting a new state of the art among "base"-sized Vietnamese encoders and demonstrating strong cross-domain generalization. We release BamiBERT at: https://huggingface.co/Qualcomm-AI-Research/BamiBERT

</details>


### [171] [CheckRLM: Effective Knowledge-Thought Coherence Checking in Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02262)
*Dingling Xu,Ruobing Wang,Qingfei Zhao,Yukun Yan,Zhichun Wang,Daren Zha,Shi Yu,Zhenghao Liu,Shuo Wang,Xu Han,Maosong Sun*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CheckRLM enhances the reliability of Reasoning Language Models by correcting factual errors in reasoning chains through a Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve the performance of RLMs in knowledge-intensive tasks by addressing factual inaccuracies that arise during reasoning.

Method: CheckRLM extracts factual claims from the reasoning process to identify inconsistencies and uses a refinement mechanism to correct errors with minimal cost using external knowledge.

Result: CheckRLM significantly outperforms existing methods in reducing error accumulation during long-horizon reasoning tasks.

Conclusion: The proposed framework effectively increases the reliability of reasoning in language models, demonstrating that structured error correction leads to improved performance.

Abstract: Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) have significantly improved performance on complex tasks by extending the reasoning chain. However, these chains are prone to containing factual errors, particularly in knowledge-intensive tasks. To address this issue, we propose CheckRLM, a framework that improves the reliability of the reasoning process through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) by timely checking and correcting factual errors. Specifically, CheckRLM extracts factual claims from the reasoning chain to identify and localize subtle knowledge inconsistencies during inference. Upon detection of errors, a refinement mechanism performs minimal-cost yet precise corrections by leveraging external knowledge, ensuring coherence between the reasoning chain and correct knowledge. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CheckRLM substantially outperforms existing baselines, exhibiting a strong capability to mitigate error accumulation in long-horizon reasoning with lower costs. The code and data are available at https://github.com/AI9Stars/CheckRLM.

</details>


### [172] [On the Role of Directionality in Structural Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02307)
*Zichao Wei*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper presents a redesigned symbolic backend using CCG directed types for the SLOG test categories, achieving improved performance over the previous state-of-the-art AM-Parser.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the shortcomings of AM-Parser's AM algebra that does not encode direction in cases where directional distinctions are critical.

Method: The authors implement a new symbolic backend based on CCG directed types using a deterministic CKY algorithm and a single linear decoder, resulting in a model with 30K learnable parameters and evaluated under a BERT-base encoder.

Result: The new system achieves a performance of 75.9$␀bpm 6.4% LF exact match, outperforming AM-Parser's 70.8$␀bpm 4.3%. Additional improvements are noted with DeBERTa-v3-large, reaching 90.7$␀bpm 4.9%.

Conclusion: Directional representations effectively shift the performance bottleneck from the symbolic layer to the neural layer, which enhances the system's capabilities when encoder upgrades are implemented.

Abstract: Several SLOG test categories explicitly involve directional distinctions (modifier position shifts, argument extraction positions), yet AM-Parser, the previous SOTA, uses an AM algebra whose operations do not encode direction. We redesign the symbolic backend around CCG directed types (deterministic CKY + single linear decoder, 30K learnable parameters). Under the same BERT-base encoder, the system achieves 75.9$\pm$6.4% LF exact match, surpassing AM-Parser (70.8$\pm$4.3%). Per SLOG's own category groupings, gains are highly directional: the CCG system outperforms AM-Parser on all 5 position-shift categories (+29.9pp), while AM-Parser outperforms on all 6 recursive-depth categories. Replacing the encoder with DeBERTa-v3-large yields 90.7$\pm$4.9%, with the largest encoder gains in recursive-depth categories, complementary to directionality's gains. Directional representations shift the bottleneck from the symbolic layer (AM-Parser's 0% category ceiling) to the neural layer, which improves with encoder upgrades.

</details>


### [173] [World Wide Models: Literary Tools for Cultural AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02369)
*Nina Begus*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper discusses the intersection between literature and AI, advocating for a framework that incorporates comparative reading and critical theory to enrich AI development.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the cultural implications of AI and its textuality in a global context.

Method: Developing a layered framework that combines literary analysis tools with AI development, focusing on macrostructure, circulation, and untranslatability.

Result: Highlights the necessity of integrating comparative literature and critical theory into AI to foster culturally aware technologies.

Conclusion: Proposes a pluralistic approach to understanding AI through literary perspectives, enhancing cultural literacy in AI.

Abstract: LLMs stage a new form of cultural encounter that is massive, automated, and monolingual. Literary disciplines have always negotiated cultural struggles with comparative reading of literature, narratological and poetic analysis, critical theory, world literature, and translation. These tools have now become indispensable for building culturally literate AI. The essay develops a layered framework toward more nuanced textual models and pluralistic interpretations of AI, emphasizing the natural intersections of literature and AI development, connecting current debates in critical theory with structural monolingualism, and suggesting a new application of world literature approaches to address global AI textuality through macrostructure, circulation, and untranslatability.

</details>


### [174] [HULAT2 at MER-TRANS 2026: Governed Multi-Agent Simplification for Spanish Easy-to-Read Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02381)
*Lourdes Moreno,Paloma Martínez,Marco Antonio Sanchez-Escudero,Miguel Domínguez-Gómez*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper reports on HULAT2-UC3M's participation in the MER-TRANS 2026 task on multilingual Easy-to-Read translation using various automated methods, with RUN1 achieving the highest performance metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The study aims to advance multilingual Easy-to-Read translation methodologies and evaluate the effectiveness of different automated approaches.

Method: The paper presents three runs: RUN1 employs a LangGraph-based workflow without lexical support; RUN2 integrates an additional lexical-support layer; RUN3 serves as a baseline using generate-evaluate-regenerate techniques.

Result: RUN1 achieved the highest SARI score of 44.0543, followed by RUN2 and RUN3, suggesting multi-agent routing is superior to traditional baselines, but lexical support doesn't guarantee better scores.

Conclusion: Further analysis is needed to evaluate readability and other qualitative factors, as current results indicate that while signal-guided approaches are effective, enhancements like lexical support need careful implementation.

Abstract: This paper describes the participation of HULAT2-UC3M in the Spanish track of MER-TRANS 2026, a shared task on multilingual Easy-to-Read translation. Three fully automatic Spanish runs were submitted. RUN1 and RUN2 used a LangGraph-based multi-agent workflow combining Gemini 2.5 Flash and RigoChat-7B-v2, parallel generation strategies, internal quality signals, Event-Condition-Action routing, controlled editing and traceable decisions. RUN1 used the base workflow, while RUN2 activated an additional lexical-support layer based on a glossary and lexical resources. RUN3 was a RigoChat-based generate-evaluate-regenerate baseline with prompt engineering and LoRA-based adaptation. The official leaderboard reports BLEU-Orig, BLEU-Gold, SARI and BERTScore. During development, additional internal signals were also inspected, including semantic fidelity, readability, lexical simplicity, syntactic clarity and factual consistency. According to official SARI, RUN1 was the best HULAT2 run, with 44.0543 points, followed by RUN2 with 43.1049 and RUN3 with 38.5136. These results indicate that, in this task setting, signal-guided multi-agent routing outperformed the linear regeneration baseline. They also show that adding lexical support did not automatically improve reference-based scores. Further segment-level and document-level analysis are required to assess readability, factual consistency and user-oriented adequacy.

</details>


### [175] [Know Your Source: A Public Knowledge Store for Media Background Checks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02383)
*Benjamin Nichols,Michael Schlichtkrull,Nedjma Ousidhoum*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduction of MEDIAREF, a knowledge store to improve MBC generation in AFC by providing low-cost, reproducible evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enhance fact-checking by addressing the unreliability of evidence sources in RAG systems, allowing for transparent justifications in automated fact-checking.

Method: Development of MEDIAREF, a publicly available knowledge store containing documents from 200 media sources, enabling an efficient methodology for MBC generation without reliance on proprietary APIs.

Result: MEDIAREF allows for reproducible assessment of MBC generation and shows improved quality in assessments from widely used LLMs.

Conclusion: MEDIAREF supports higher-quality MBC generation, enhancing the reliability of evidence in automated fact-checking systems.

Abstract: LLM-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is increasingly used for automated fact-checking (AFC) and related tasks. By grounding LLM outputs in retrieved evidence, RAG-based systems provide transparent justifications while allowing external information to be updated independently of the underlying model. However, existing approaches often assume retrieved evidence is reliable, although real-world information may be conflicting, outdated, and can originate from unreliable or biased sources. Recent work on *source-critical reasoning* addresses this challenge through media background checks (MBCs) (Schlichtkrull, 2024), which assess the credibility of evidence sources to support downstream fact verification. However, generating MBCs relies on costly proprietary search APIs, limiting reproducibility. To mitigate this issue, we introduce MEDIAREF, a publicly available knowledge store of web-sourced documents that enables reproducible, low-cost evaluation of MBC generation across 200 media sources. We describe a reproducible methodology for constructing and updating the collection, assess widely used LLMs on the MBC generation task, and demonstrate that MEDIAREF supports higher-quality MBC generation through both automatic and qualitative evaluation.

</details>


### [176] [The Future of NLP may not be at NLP Conferences: Scholarly Migration Patterns in Natural Language Processing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02416)
*David Jurgens*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The study analyzes the shifting publication trends in NLP, revealing a decline in established authors' presence at traditional ACL venues, a rise in general ML venues, and a growing citation premium associated with general ML publications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether the disciplinary focus of NLP research is changing due to advances in LLMs and evolving author publishing behavior.

Method: Analysis of NLP research publication trends from 2010 to 2026, comparing pre- and post-LLM era data, and utilizing causal inference techniques to assess citation impacts.

Result: Established authors' share at ACL venues decreased, while general ML venues saw an increase; newer authors are publishing more in general ML venues compared to ACL.

Conclusion: These trends indicate a significant shift in the publication landscape for NLP research, with implications for future research visibility and impact.

Abstract: Natural Language Processing (NLP) has traditionally been published in its core disciplinary venues like ACL. However, advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) has led to a blurring of the disciplinary lines between NLP and general Machine Learning (ML), with authors regularly publishing in venues from both fields. Here, we ask whether the disciplinary center of gravity is shifting. Using NLP research published from 2010 to 2026 and studies of both established and new authors, we find that a migration is taking place. First, comparing the pre- and post-LLM eras, established authors lost 19.2pp of share at flagship *ACL main-conference tracks while gaining 14.8pp in the newer Findings tracks, and general ML venues rose 8.6pp, even when adjusting for parallel growth in the fields. Second, among newer authors who debut with at least three first-author NLP-topic papers, the share whose work appears mostly at *ACL venues fell from 84% (2019) to 74% (2024), while the share appearing mostly at general ML venues rose from 5% to 21%. Using causal inference techniques, we estimate that these general ML venues confer a significant citation premium, which influences venue selection. Together, these results point to a significant shift in where NLP research is published.

</details>


### [177] [Language Models as Measurement Apparatus for Culture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02459)
*Kent K. Chang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper explores the ways in which language models interact with cultural phenomena, emphasizing that these models not only measure but also shape cultural realities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate how language models serve as both instruments and constituents of cultural measurement in NLP, highlighting their active role in shaping cultural understanding.

Method: The author analyzes the apparatus involved in NLP work on culture through the lens of Karen Barad's concept of the agential cut, using case studies of television and film dialogue to illustrate this relationship.

Result: The study reveals that the design choices in language models influence cultural boundaries and that these models have already internalized significant cultural elements.

Conclusion: The paper advocates for a research approach that is rigorous, theory-driven, and ethically aware of the cultural implications of technology, recognizing agential cuts as both methodological and ethical commitments.

Abstract: Language models are increasingly used to quantify cultural phenomena, but what makes such measurement distinctively cultural? This paper argues that NLP work on culture is a material-discursive practice: the apparatus -- model, data, annotation, evaluation -- participates in constituting the cultural reality it measures, rather than passively recording it. Drawing on Karen Barad's concept of the agential cut -- the contingent boundary between phenomenon and instrument -- I show that the apparatus's substantive design choices draw such boundaries, and that the boundary is entangled from the start because language models have already internalized much of the cultural material they measure. I illustrate this through three case studies on television and film dialogue (measuring structure, interaction, and deviation) and three examinations of the apparatus itself (erasure of cultural markers, attunement to historical material, and agency in an agentic workflow). This big picture analysis proposes a research program that is theory-driven, empirically rigorous, and culturally contingent, treating each agential cut as a conscious commitment, at once methodological and ethical.

</details>


### [178] [Will Scaling Improve Social Simulation with LLMs?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02464)
*Caleb Ziems,William Held,Su Doga Karaca,David Grusky,Tatsunori Hashimoto,Diyi Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This study examines the effectiveness of scaling Large Language Models (LLMs) in improving social simulation fidelity across various domains, revealing that while some tasks benefit from scale, others, especially low-resource domains, do not.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To assess if the scaling of LLMs can enhance the fidelity of social simulations and identify areas needing further research.

Method: The authors employ scaling laws to analyze the compute scale of 85 transformer LLMs across tasks in opinion modeling, behavioral simulation, and longitudinal forecasting, using a diverse corpus and a range of model sizes up to 70B parameters.

Result: The study finds strong scaling effects in opinion modeling and behavioral simulations, while longitudinal forecasting and less-represented opinions exhibit slower scaling improvements, particularly in correlation with general knowledge and reasoning benchmarks.

Conclusion: Scaling generally enhances performance in social simulations, but limitations exist in certain tasks, particularly in underrepresented areas, suggesting that future research should focus on these outliers.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) social simulations are a promising research method, but they are not yet faithful enough to be adopted widely. In this work, we investigate whether the current scaling paradigm in language modeling is likely to close these gaps, or whether simulation fidelity is orthogonal to general capabilities and therefore deserving of more research attention. We use scaling laws to study the relationship between LLMs' compute scale, general capability benchmarks, and the fidelity of social simulation in three representative sub-domains: opinion modeling, behavioral simulation, and longitudinal forecasting. Surprisingly, we discover strong compute scaling in all three settings, using a suite of 85 transformer LLMs with the Qwen3 architecture pre-trained on the DCLM web text corpus under fixed-compute budgets from $10^{18}$ to $10^{20}$ FLOPs. Then we evaluate 35 larger and more capable open-weight models up to 70B parameters, allowing us to predict downstream accuracy from loss. This reveals that the majority of behavioral and opinion simulation tasks will rapidly improve with scale, particularly when they involve populations that are well-represented in English web corpora. Longitudinal forecasting and underrepresented opinions scale more slowly, especially when they are less correlated with general knowledge and reasoning benchmarks like MMLU. In behavior simulation, scaling fails to improve model calibration with human cognitive biases like risk aversion, as well as human heuristics like learning correlated rewards from related tasks. On these tasks, even fine-tuned models fail to noticeably scale up performance from 0.5B to 8B parameters. Taken together, we conclude that scale will improve social simulations in most settings, but outliers exist, and improvements will be less reliable in low-resource domains.

</details>


### [179] [Audio-Based Understanding of Audiobook Narration Appeal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02473)
*Shahar Elisha,Mariano Beguerisse-Díaz,Emmanouil Benetos*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates how narration qualities in audiobooks influence listener engagement and appeal, using vocal and acoustic features along with consumption data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the impact of narration qualities on audiobook appeal, which can differ by genre and audience.

Method: Extraction of vocal and acoustic features from LibriVox using pre-trained audio models, analyzing their relationship with view-rate consumption data and validating with proprietary engagement metrics.

Result: Acoustic features show a strong association with audiobook appeal, independent of title effects, revealing significant insights into listener preferences.

Conclusion: The study establishes a foundational link between narration qualities and audiobook consumption, suggesting data-driven methods for enhancing audiobook personalization and narrator selection.

Abstract: Narration is central to the audiobook listening experience, shaping how listeners engage with and understand the content. This work explores how narration qualities shape an audiobook's appeal, noting that their effects can vary by genre, title, and audience. We extract vocal and acoustic features (e.g., tone, pace, loudness) from LibriVox using pre-trained audio models and analyse their relationship with consumption data (specifically, view-rate) and their interplay with genre and title. Despite limited consumption data, we find that acoustic information alone has a robust association with appeal, even after accounting for title effects. We further validate these findings using more nuanced proprietary engagement metrics. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic computational study linking narration qualities, genre, title, and audiobook consumption, highlighting the potential of data-driven insights to improve audiobook personalisation and narrator casting.

</details>


### [180] [Visually Grounded Self-Reflection for Vision-Language Models via Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02490)
*Liyan Tang,Fangcong Yin,Greg Durrett*

Main category: cs.CL
